prize_parts.citation: for the invention and development of the optical lattice clock, enabling measurement of time and frequency at the 10^-18 level

statement.case_for: I opened with the Event Horizon Telescope, and I still think it is the discovery with the greatest existential reach on the list. But reading the whole table I have to separate how much a discovery moves me from how well a prize can be built on it. The optical lattice clock is the one entry every member ranked, six of eight in their top three, and the scientific arguments are consistent and independent of one another. Katori's magic-wavelength insight removes the lattice light shift while many atoms are held in the Lamb-Dicke regime, and Ye's group turned that into clocks at the 1e-18 level with a many-body understanding of the systematics. The result is an instrument that questions nature directly: gravitational redshift across millimetres, limits on drifting constants and on ultralight dark matter, and a redefinition of the second that is now being prepared around such clocks. That is a clue-from-nature machine, not an elegant model. The attribution is also the cleanest on the shortlist: two names, concept plus record demonstration, no forced choice among members of a collaboration of hundreds. Given the committee's habit of putting the discovery first and then asking who stands behind it, here the people are unusually easy to find.
statement.case_against: The strongest reservation is that this is partly a precision-measurement advance, one step from the 2005 frequency-comb prize and the 2012 trapped-ion prize, and some will say it is metrology rather than a new phenomenon. The clock lineage also has other legitimate claimants (Lemonde, Takamoto, Hollberg, the Yb and Hg groups), and Katori and Ye have collaborated and competed in ways I cannot fully adjudicate from the supplied text. The redefinition of the second is still pending, so one could argue for waiting. Finally, I am giving up my own first choice: if the committee values the sheer cosmic significance of a discovery over attributional tidiness, the EHT is more striking than a clock, and I accept that I am trading some excitement for defensibility.

responses.point: The magic-wavelength lattice clock combines an original idea with a decisive precision leap and is a deep atomic-physics result that becomes a new measurement capability, though she asks whether it is distinct enough from the 2005 and 2012 prizes.
responses.response: I agree with the case and I think the distinctness question has a good answer. The 2005 prize recognised the comb as a ruler for optical frequencies and the 2012 prize recognised control of single quantum systems. Neither delivers the thing Katori proposed, a Doppler- and recoil-free ensemble of many atoms that gives statistical power and accuracy together. That is what took clocks from 1e-16 to 1e-18 and opened the many-body regime. I would hold the citation to the lattice clock itself, so it does not read as a third prize for the same lineage, and I would not let the ion-clock community's role blur that line.

responses.point: He ranks the IceCube neutrino discovery first, resting the case on the diffuse flux rather than the statistically modest TXS 0506+056 association, and he has reservations about the credit in the EHT triple because of collaboration size and imaging-algorithm leaders.
responses.response: I take both points seriously. On the EHT, his attribution worry has moved me more than any other argument: Falcke, Doeleman and Zensus are a defensible triple, but the image itself rests on calibration and imaging work by many people outside it, and I am not confident the committee could document a fair split. On IceCube I agree the case should rest on the diffuse flux, which is secure, but I would press back that the origin of that flux is still unresolved and the source identifications are at the few-sigma level. I find it a strong and likely a coming prize, but a little less complete than the clock, and the Halzen and Karle pair leaves other project leaders uncounted, which is a larger gap than anything on the clock side.

responses.point: She ranks the experimental Higgs discovery first as a decisive experimental result not yet recognised, while admitting that choosing three names out of four from ATLAS and CMS is a judgement that leaves one credible person out.
responses.response: Her scientific argument is the best on the list: the Higgs is the clearest case of nature answering a question posed by theory, and it is fully mature. My difficulty is not merit but whether the statutes and the committee's own tradition allow us to credit the leaders of two experiments with thousands of members, and whether the choice of Jenni, Virdee, Gianotti or Della Negra can be justified with documents rather than seniority. Following the 2013 prize, I would also like us to ask whether recognising the experiments is better done as a pairing. I do not see that as a reason to rank it low, but it is why I cannot put it ahead of a candidate whose credit is not in doubt. I would be glad to see her make the attribution case in more detail.

responses.point: He puts topological insulators first, as a conceptually clean new class of matter, with theory (Kane, Mele) and experiment (Molenkamp) forming a natural three-person prize.
responses.response: I accept the importance, and I see why he favours it. My worry is the attribution that he himself flags: if Bernevig, Hughes and Zhang proposed HgTe and Fu, Kane and Mele and Moore and Balents did the three-dimensional case, a Kane-Mele-Molenkamp prize leaves out people whom many in the field would consider essential, and the 2016 prize has already honoured topology in matter. I do not think that is fatal, but it makes a tidy two-person clock prize easier to defend in this year's discussion.

uncertainties: Whether the committee regards the optical lattice clock as a distinct discovery or as an extension of the 2005 and 2012 clock-related prizes.
Whether the pending SI redefinition of the second makes this year the right time, or whether recognition should wait for it.

The relative weighting of Katori's original proposal and Ye's later precision milestones, and the claims of other clock groups, which I am recalling from memory and have not verified against documents.
Whether the EHT credit problem can be resolved by external expert evaluation, which would change my view of B052.
statement.conflict_note: No specific conflict is apparent from my profile for the shortlisted candidates. My supervisor David Gross and my collaborator Thomas Van Riet are not connected to any shortlisted candidate or their groups, as far as I know. I have a theoretical interest in black holes and cosmology, which bears on B052 and B008 as an intellectual preference but not a personal tie.
